newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-FIERCE COMPETITIVE FIRE STILL BURNS IN STEFFI GRAF.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-FIERCE COMPETITIVE FIRE STILL BURNS IN STEFFI GRAF.

text.p: After all the miles and strokes and titles, and with nothing left to prove, the competitive fires still burn bright in tennis superstar Steffi Graf.

While other elite players, such as Andre Agassi and Pete Sampras, complain that the sport needs more of an off-season, a break from the globe-trotting grind, the women's world number one can't wait to get back on the tennis court.

"I love travelling, I think it's one of the things that I enjoy most," Graf said during a recent lunch with a group of reporters to promote the WTA Tour's season-ending Chase Championship at Madison Square Garden starting November 18.
"I was in Germany since the (U.S.) Open, which is probably seven weeks now. I was getting so restless, I was so excited to be on the plane. It was such a beautiful feeling actually."
Graf has not played since losing a semifinal in Leipzig the first week of October due to a nagging left knee injury, one of the many aches and pains that have plagued the 27-year-old in recent years.
"During the period that I didn't play the last few weeks, I missed being able to compete," said Graf, who returns to the tennis wars this week for a tournament in Philadelphia.
Graf is looking forward to testing her incomparable skills against all comers, but admitted to being somewhat disappointed by the level of competition out there today.

"I am very surprised that with the physical problems that I've been having over the past two and a half years, with as little as I've been able to practice, to still have this kind of success," she said.
"Obviously I'm thrilled to have the results...but I do have to say that the competition is not as strong as it should be and I am sometimes disappointed that there isn't a higher standard.
"I know I'm not training as much as I could. I'm not very well prepared at most tournaments and still they can't beat me, it is strange."
She does like the fresh attitude and touch of arrogance she has seen in some of the rising, young stars like Martina Hingis. "I think that's very good to see, it will definitely help the sport."
Graf insisted that she never thinks about records, her ranking or her place in tennis history.
"When I turned number one the first time (in August, 1987) it was awesome ... but after that I never had the same feeling again."
But she does continue to amaze herself with her ability to win big tournaments despite injuries and the personal anguish from her father being imprisoned and on trial on tax evasion charges.
"I feel awkward talking about it because I'm still in the sport too much to look at what I've achieved already.

"But obviously with the numbers that came up this year, winning 21 Grand Slams, more than 100 titles, these are numbers that I'm astonished that I've achieved," said Graf, who won the French Open, Wimbledon and U.S. Open, marking the fifth time she has claimed at least three of the four majors in a single year.
Graf said she has never had specific goals or a sense of history, that a pure love of tennis keeps her going.
"It's just the game itself. The motivation is still really high. It's still a pleasure to play and why I am still in the sport, because it means so much to me."
She was surprised and a little saddened by the sudden retirement of her contemporary and longtime rival Gabriela Sabatini, who no longer shares Graf's desire to compete.
"She's somebody that I've had so many competitive years with that it's sad to see somebody leave before you ... especially since she's younger," Graf said laughing.

"It definitely made me look back on the matches that we've had. We've played each other 30 or 40 times, something like that. We had a lot of close three-setters," recalled Graf who holds a 29-11 career record against the Argentine.
"I think she had a career that she can be proud of and if she thought it was the right time (to retire), I respect her."

Graf last year called the 1995 season the most personally satisfying of her career. But after duplicating her three major titles while dealing with the emotional rollercoaster of her father's situation, Graf rated 1996 even higher.
"Obviously, I had a lot of injuries and problems last year, but I think this year probably was the limit that I could go to," she admitted.
Graf talked about coming into Wimbledon and the U.S. Open "tense and nervous" because of lack of practice due to injury, but somehow finding a way to win.
And she enthusiastically recalled the roar of the crowd during the classic French Open final, which she won from Arantxa Sanchez Vicario 10-8 in the third set.
"To be in a match like that, I've never been in a match that the people got so strongly into it.
"These are memories that I will always treasure and I think that's what makes this year so special."
